newsitem.title: USA: Chance of Democratic sweep has US bond mkt on edge.
newsitem.headline: Chance of Democratic sweep has US bond mkt on edge.

text.p: The odds of a Democratic sweep in upcoming Congressional elections may be slim, but the mounting chance of such a result has Treasury market participants quaking.

The market is confident that President Clinton will beat Republican rival Bob Dole quite handily on November 5, and is comfortable with another four years of Democratic leadership in the executive office.

But should the Democrats also retake the House and perhaps pull to even strength in the Senate, it's a good bet Treasury spreads would widen, with the long end of the yield curve taking the brunt of the market's displeasure, experts said.

"Clinton winning is not bad for the market if the Republicans retain control of Congress," said James Kenney, head trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "Clinton and the Democrats winning (the Senate) will be a negative to the market."

With just five days until the election, the two-to-30-year spread stood at roughly 90 basis points. If the presidential and Congressional status quo remained intact, experts said, the market could get a slight boost across the curve.

At present, Republicans have a 235-197 majority in the House, with one independent and two vacancies. They also have a slim 53-47 margin in the Senate. Numerous polls give solid odds to the Democrats regaining a majority in the House, for which they would need to pick up 19 seats.
A landslide win by Clinton could give the Democrats an even bigger margin in the House, although it would be tougher to win back the Senate, most players agreed.

"If the Democrats take back both houses, it will be troubling enough to people that bonds will sell off and the yield curve will probably steepen," said Bruce Steinberg, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc.

"But even with that outcome -- which is not the most likely -- the Republicans will still have a major (presence)," he added. "The market realizes that no one really has effective control and not much would change."

Still, some noted that liberal-leaning Democratic Congressmen Charles Rangel of New York, who would be chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, and Richard Gephardt of Missouri, the likely speaker of the House, could be a problem.

"The idea of Rangel and Gephardt being influential becomes scary," said Michael Strauss, executive vice president and chief economist at Yamaichi International (America) Inc. "It may not sit too well with market participants."
He said Gephardt, for one, is an opponent of the recently signed free trade agreements, which could lead to trade battles with Japan and China.
Prudential's Kenney, meanwhile, said the market would prefer not to dwell on that possibility.

The status quo "is good for the market because there will probably be some work on the (budget) deficit, they'll address entitlememts and there will be no increases in (government) spending," he said.
But a Democrat-controlled House, he said, would be problematic because of their "tax and spend" formula.
"There will be a bigger deficit, a worsening inflation outlook and less ... work on entitlements. So, that is the fear."
Given those expectations, there would be renewed fears of a Fed tightening, he added.
Yet, no matter what the outcome, many don't expect a huge reaction beyond the initial trades.

"Right now, the market is paying attention to numbers, numbers, numbers," said Steven Ricchiuto, chief financial economist at BZW Securities Inc, referring to the slew of key economic reports on tap. "It's the numbers, stupid!"
